title: Seeing things sideways
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1448, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 1448 · constellation Horologium · about 50 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: NGC 1448 looks like a glittering oval rather than the round spiral many people picture. It is a spiral galaxy in the little-known constellation Horologium, the Pendulum Clock, about 50 million light-years from Earth, and was photographed by Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3.

The oval shape comes down to viewing angle. The source compares a spiral galaxy to a frisbee spinning slowly in space. When one faces us, we can see a great deal of its detail and structure, as in Hubble's well-known view of Messier 51, the Whirlpool Galaxy.

NGC 1448 is tipped almost edge-on to Earth, so its disc looks squeezed into an oval. The spiral arms still curve out from its dense core, and in Hubble's image they can just about be made out. Seen face-on, NGC 1448 would look far rounder, like the Whirlpool.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.68 x 2.38 arcminutes) and distance (50 million light years), the frame spans roughly 39,000 × 35,000 light-years. Its light set out about 50 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 1448 in visible light through filters at 350, 555 and 814 nm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's exposures reach far fainter light than an eye at a telescope, bringing out the arms that are hard to see in such a tilted galaxy.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

alt: An elongated, nearly edge-on spiral galaxy with a dense core and faint arms curving out from it.
